## Module 6: Welcome back

Modules 1 through 5 got you comfortable installing R, running and reading code, and cleaning up and plotting real data. From here on, the work looks a little different: instead of writing the code that produces a result, you'll often be handed a script someone else wrote -- an instructor, a teammate, an AI assistant -- and asked to run it and make sense of what it produced.

This module is about that second skill: given some model's output, can you tell whether it's a good fit, and whether one model is better than another? None of this asks you to build a model yourself -- just to read the numbers and plots a model produces, the same way you've been reading error messages and grader feedback all course.

## Module 6: Is it a line, or a curve?

The most basic question you can ask about a relationship between two numbers -- like a fish's length and its weight -- is whether it looks like a straight line or a curve. This matters because a model that assumes a straight line (like the ones you'll see below) will systematically miss if the real relationship curves.

```{r linear-demo, echo=TRUE, fig.height=3}
plot(demo_linear_x, demo_linear_y, main = "Relationship A", xlab = "x", ylab = "y", pch = 19, col = "steelblue")
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
quiz_question_ui("linear_shape_quiz", "Look at \"Relationship A\" above. Does it look like a straight line or a curve?", c(
  "A straight line" = "correct",
  "A curve" = "wrong_curve"
))
```

```{r curved-demo, echo=TRUE, fig.height=3}
plot(demo_curved_x, demo_curved_y, main = "Relationship B", xlab = "x", ylab = "y", pch = 19, col = "darkorange")
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
quiz_question_ui("curved_shape_quiz", "Look at \"Relationship B\" above. Does it look like a straight line or a curve?", c(
  "A curve" = "correct",
  "A straight line" = "wrong_line"
))
```

## Module 6: R-squared -- how much does this explain?

**R-squared (R^2^)** is a number between 0 and 1 that says how much of the up-and-down variation in the outcome a model actually accounts for:

$$
R^2 = 1 - \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\text{actual}_i - \text{predicted}_i)^2}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\text{actual}_i - \overline{\text{actual}})^2}
$$

The bottom of the fraction is how much the actual values vary on their own (compared to their average, $\overline{\text{actual}}$); the top is how much of that variation the model's predictions still miss. Subtracting that ratio from 1 turns "fraction still missed" into "fraction explained."

An R^2^ of 0 means the model explains essentially nothing; an R^2^ of 1 means it explains all of it (rare, and often a sign something's off). Closer to 1 is generally better, but it's not the whole story -- a model can have a high R^2^ and still be the wrong shape (a straight line squeezed through curved data can still post a middling-to-decent R^2^ while clearly missing the pattern), which is why you look at both the number and the shape.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
quiz_question_ui("r_squared_quiz", "A model has an R-squared of 0.85. Another model, on the same data, has an R-squared of 0.20. Which model is explaining more of the variation in the outcome?", c(
  "The one with R-squared = 0.85" = "correct",
  "The one with R-squared = 0.20" = "wrong_low",
  "They're explaining the same amount" = "wrong_same"
))
```

## Module 6: RMSE -- how far off are the guesses?

**RMSE (root mean squared error)** answers a more concrete question: on average, how far off is the model's prediction from the real value?

$$
\text{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\text{actual}_i - \text{predicted}_i)^2}
$$

$n$ is how many predictions there are, and $\text{actual}_i$/$\text{predicted}_i$ are the real and predicted value for the $i$-th one. In words: for each prediction, subtract to see how far off it was, square those differences (so a miss in either direction counts, and big misses count extra), average the squared differences, then take the square root to get back to the original units.

It's in the *same units* as whatever you're predicting -- an RMSE of 12 grams means the model's guesses are typically off by around 12 grams. Lower RMSE means smaller, better predictions.

### Practice: compute RMSE

Below, `actual_weights` and `predicted_weights` are two vectors of the same length -- real fish weights, and a model's predictions for those same fish. Compute the RMSE: the square root of the mean of the squared differences between them. Replace the `FIXME`.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
exercise_ui("rmse_exercise", "differences <- actual_weights - predicted_weights\nsqrt(mean(differences^FIXME))")
```

## Module 6: Comparing two models

Once you can compute RMSE (or read an R^2^) for a model, comparing two models on the *same* data and the *same* outcome is just a matter of comparing the numbers: lower RMSE wins, higher R^2^ wins. Two things trip people up here, though:

- **RMSE is only comparable in the same units.** A model predicting weight in grams and one predicting weight in kilograms will have very different-looking RMSEs even if they're equally good -- you can't compare across different units or different outcomes.
- **Always look at both models on the same held-out data.** A model that looks great on the data it was built from can still do worse on new data it hasn't seen -- which is exactly why the capstone script coming up tests each model on fish it wasn't shown.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
quiz_question_ui("rmse_compare_quiz", "Model A has an RMSE of 12 grams. Model B has an RMSE of 40 grams, predicting the same fish's weight. Which model's predictions are typically closer to the truth?", c(
  "Model A" = "correct",
  "Model B" = "wrong_b",
  "Can't tell without also knowing R-squared" = "wrong_r2"
))
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
quiz_question_ui("rmse_units_quiz", "Why can't you directly compare an RMSE of 0.03 (predicting weight in kilograms) to an RMSE of 30 (predicting weight in grams) and conclude the first model is way better?", c(
  "RMSE is in the same units as what's being predicted, and kilograms and grams aren't directly comparable" = "correct",
  "You can -- RMSE is unitless, so smaller is always better regardless of units" = "wrong_unitless",
  "RMSE only works correctly when the units are grams" = "wrong_grams"
))
```

## Module 6: Wrapping up

That covers the basics of judging model output -- none of it required building a model yourself, just the vocabulary and habits to make sense of one you're handed.

**If you remember only a few things from this module:**

- Look at the shape of the data before trusting a straight-line model -- a curve squeezed into a line will systematically miss.
- RMSE is in the *same units* as what you're predicting, and lower is better; R^2^ is a 0-1 fraction of variation explained, and closer to 1 is better.
- Always compare two models on the same held-out data they weren't trained on -- looking good on data a model has already seen doesn't count.

That's exactly what the capstone preview coming up asks you to do: a real script fits two models to real fish data and prints their RMSE, and your job is to read that output and decide what it's telling you.

```{r setup-module7, context="setup", include=FALSE}
# Question generators for the Extra Practice module, one per module (2-6)
# for this BETA version -- one question type per module, deliberately
# mirroring content that module already teaches. A later pass (after beta
# feedback) will add MORE generators per module, including types not tied
# to any of that module's actual graded exercises, per the app owner's
# explicit direction: practice questions should draw on everything a
# module taught, not just repeat its existing exercise shapes.
#
# Each generator is a zero-argument function, called fresh every time a new
# question is requested (a module switch or a "New Question" click),
# returning list(prompt=, starting_code=, check=). See module_practice_ui()/
# module_practice_server() in R/tutor_utils.R for the full contract -- in
# particular, why the random values below are baked directly into
# `prompt`/`starting_code` as literal text rather than stored in a shared
# variable: this data is per-question, not identical across every student's
# session the way e.g. Module 4's fish_clean is, so it can't safely live in
# globalenv() the way that reference data does.

generate_module2_practice <- function() {
  keep_msg <- sample(c("Keep this one running", "Do not touch this line", "This line should stay active"), 1)
  comment_msg <- sample(c("Turn this into a comment", "This line should not run", "Comment this one out"), 1)

  list(
    prompt = sprintf('Below, comment out the SECOND line only (the one that says "%s"), so it does not run -- without deleting it or changing the first line.', comment_msg),
    starting_code = sprintf('print("%s")\nprint("%s")', keep_msg, comment_msg),
    check = function(user_code, result, envir) {
      keep_active <- grepl(paste0('(?m)^\\s*print\\("', keep_msg, '"\\)\\s*$'), user_code, perl = TRUE)
      comment_present <- grepl(paste0('(?m)^\\s*#.*', comment_msg), user_code, perl = TRUE)
      comment_still_active <- grepl(paste0('(?m)^\\s*print\\("', comment_msg, '"\\)\\s*$'), user_code, perl = TRUE)
      passed <- keep_active && comment_present && !comment_still_active

      message <- if (passed) {
        "Correct -- the first line still runs, and the second is safely commented out."
      } else if (!keep_active) {
        "The first line got changed or removed -- it should stay exactly as it was."
      } else if (comment_still_active) {
        "The second line is still active R code -- put a # in front of it to comment it out."
      } else {
        "Add a # before the second line to comment it out."
      }
      list(passed = passed, message = message)
    }
  )
}

generate_module3_practice <- function() {
  n <- sample(4:7, 1)
  values <- sample(1:50, n)
  idx <- sample(seq_len(n), 1)
  correct <- values[idx]
  value_str <- paste(values, collapse = ", ")

  list(
    prompt = sprintf(
      "Given practice_vec <- c(%s), write code that returns the value at position %d.",
      value_str, idx
    ),
    starting_code = sprintf("practice_vec <- c(%s)\npractice_vec[FIXME]", value_str),
    check = function(user_code, result, envir) {
      uses_index <- grepl("\\[", user_code)
      correct_result <- is.numeric(result) && length(result) == 1 && isTRUE(result == correct)
      passed <- uses_index && correct_result

      message <- if (passed) {
        sprintf("Correct -- position %d is %d.", idx, correct)
      } else if (!uses_index) {
        "Use square brackets (like practice_vec[FIXME]) to index into the vector."
      } else {
        sprintf("Not quite -- double check you're asking for position %d specifically.", idx)
      }
      list(passed = passed, message = message)
    }
  )
}

generate_module4_practice <- function() {
  fruits <- sample(c("apple", "banana", "cherry", "date", "elderberry"), sample(3:4, 1))
  n <- length(fruits) * 2
  fruit_col <- sample(fruits, n, replace = TRUE)
  count_col <- sample(5:40, n)
  target_fruit <- sample(fruits, 1)
  correct <- sum(count_col[fruit_col == target_fruit])
  fruit_str <- paste(sprintf('"%s"', fruit_col), collapse = ", ")
  count_str <- paste(count_col, collapse = ", ")

  list(
    prompt = sprintf(
      'practice_df has a fruit column and a count column. Using dplyr, filter down to just "%s" and compute the total (sum) of count.',
      target_fruit
    ),
    starting_code = sprintf(
      'practice_df <- data.frame(fruit = c(%s), count = c(%s))\npractice_df |>\n  filter(fruit == FIXME) |>\n  summarize(total = sum(count))',
      fruit_str, count_str
    ),
    check = function(user_code, result, envir) {
      uses_filter <- grepl("filter\\s*\\(", user_code)
      is_df <- is.data.frame(result) && "total" %in% names(result)
      correct_result <- is_df && isTRUE(all.equal(result$total, correct))
      passed <- uses_filter && correct_result

      message <- if (passed) {
        sprintf("Correct -- the total count for %s is %d.", target_fruit, correct)
      } else if (!uses_filter) {
        sprintf('Use filter(fruit == "%s") to keep just those rows first.', target_fruit)
      } else if (!is_df) {
        "This should end up as a summarized table with a total column -- check the summarize() step."
      } else {
        sprintf('Not quite -- double check the filter is matching "%s" exactly.', target_fruit)
      }
      list(passed = passed, message = message)
    }
  )
}

generate_module5_practice <- function() {
  n <- sample(15:25, 1)
  x_vals <- round(runif(n, 1, 50), 1)
  y_vals <- round(x_vals * runif(1, 0.5, 2) + rnorm(n, sd = 5), 1)
  x_str <- paste(x_vals, collapse = ", ")
  y_str <- paste(y_vals, collapse = ", ")

  list(
    prompt = "practice_df has columns x and y. Create a scatter plot with x on the x-axis and y on the y-axis.",
    starting_code = sprintf(
      "practice_df <- data.frame(x = c(%s), y = c(%s))\nggplot(practice_df, aes(x = FIXME, y = FIXME)) +\n  geom_point()",
      x_str, y_str
    ),
    check = function(user_code, result, envir) {
      uses_geom_point <- grepl("geom_point\\s*\\(", user_code)
      is_ggplot <- inherits(result, "ggplot")
      has_point_layer <- is_ggplot && any(vapply(result$layers, function(l) inherits(l$geom, "GeomPoint"), logical(1)))
      x_ok <- is_ggplot && identical(rlang::as_label(result$mapping$x), "x")
      y_ok <- is_ggplot && identical(rlang::as_label(result$mapping$y), "y")
      passed <- uses_geom_point && is_ggplot && has_point_layer && x_ok && y_ok

      message <- if (passed) {
        "Correct -- that's a scatter plot of x vs. y."
      } else if (!is_ggplot) {
        "This should produce a ggplot object -- make sure ggplot(practice_df, aes(...)) still starts the expression."
      } else if (!has_point_layer) {
        "This needs a geom_point() layer to draw the scatter plot."
      } else if (!x_ok) {
        "The x-axis isn't mapped to x yet -- check aes()'s x argument."
      } else {
        "Close -- the y-axis isn't mapped to y yet, check aes()'s y argument."
      }
      list(passed = passed, message = message)
    }
  )
}

generate_module6_practice <- function() {
  n <- sample(4:6, 1)
  actual <- sample(20:200, n)
  predicted <- actual + sample(-15:15, n, replace = TRUE)
  correct <- sqrt(mean((actual - predicted)^2))
  actual_str <- paste(actual, collapse = ", ")
  predicted_str <- paste(predicted, collapse = ", ")

  list(
    prompt = "practice_actual and practice_predicted are a model's actual and predicted values for the same cases. Compute the RMSE.",
    starting_code = sprintf(
      "practice_actual <- c(%s)\npractice_predicted <- c(%s)\nsqrt(mean((practice_actual - practice_predicted)^FIXME))",
      actual_str, predicted_str
    ),
    check = function(user_code, result, envir) {
      correct_result <- is.numeric(result) && length(result) == 1 && isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(result), correct, tolerance = 0.01))
      message <- if (correct_result) {
        sprintf("Correct -- RMSE is about %.2f.", correct)
      } else {
        "Not quite -- check the RMSE formula: square the differences, average them, then take the square root."
      }
      list(passed = correct_result, message = message)
    }
  )
}

MODULE_PRACTICE_GENERATORS <- list(
  "2" = list(generate_fn = generate_module2_practice, has_plot_output = FALSE),
  "3" = list(generate_fn = generate_module3_practice, has_plot_output = FALSE),
  "4" = list(generate_fn = generate_module4_practice, has_plot_output = FALSE),
  "5" = list(generate_fn = generate_module5_practice, has_plot_output = TRUE),
  "6" = list(generate_fn = generate_module6_practice, has_plot_output = FALSE)
)
```

```{r, context="server"}
# --- Practice chat + exercise wiring --------------------------------------
# NEW GOTCHA, found building this module: module_practice_ui()'s panel is
# entirely dynamic (a bare uiOutput(), filled in by renderUI() after the
# session starts) -- unlike every other exercise/quiz in this app, which
# emit fully static HTML at knit time (only their small feedback area is a
# uiOutput()). An earlier version of this module stacked two such dynamic
# panels as separate `###` sub-sections under one `##` topic, which
# silently broke learnr's progressive/allow_skip "Continue" gate between
# them -- it never unlocked no matter what was submitted, confirmed via the
# DOM directly (the locked `###` stayed a `display: none`
# `.section.level3.hide` div). Root cause, as best determined: that gate
# depends on markup present in the static HTML at knit time to recognize a
# section's exercise as completed, which a bare uiOutput() placeholder
# doesn't provide regardless of what's later rendered into it. Since this
# module is ungraded anyway (no reason to force sequential completion), the
# fix is to not use `###` subheadings for this content at all -- see the
# bold-text label below instead of `###`. Any FUTURE dynamic-UI content
# stacked under one `##` topic should do the same (flat, no `###`) unless
# this gets solved.
#
# One shared, ungraded practice chat for the whole module (not per-question
# -- there's no fixed exercise context to hang a separate panel off of).
wire_standalone_chat("tutor_chat_m7_practice", "tutor_accordion_m7_practice", "Ask for practice help", PRACTICE_SYSTEM_PROMPT, PRACTICE_CHAT_GREETING, input, output, session)

module_practice_server(input, output, session, "module_practice", MODULE_PRACTICE_GENERATORS)
```

## Module 7: Extra Practice

Everything up to here has been graded, one-shot content -- pass it once and move on. This module is different: it's **ungraded and endlessly repeatable**. Pick a module below and click "New Question" for a fresh version any time, as many times as you want, whenever you want more reps on a skill. Nothing here is tracked or scored -- it's just practice.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
accordion(
  id = "tutor_accordion_m7_practice",
  open = FALSE,
  accordion_panel(
    title = "Ask for practice help",
    chat_ui(
      "tutor_chat_m7_practice",
      placeholder = "Ask a question, or paste your current practice question or code...",
      greeting = PRACTICE_CHAT_GREETING,
      allow_attachments = FALSE
    )
  )
)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
module_practice_ui("module_practice", c(
  "Module 2" = "2", "Module 3" = "3", "Module 4" = "4", "Module 5" = "5", "Module 6" = "6"
))
```
